items.stimulus:
Today a restaurant seems an obvious idea: you choose a time, sit at your own table, pick dishes from a printed list and pay a stated price for what you ate. Yet in Paris this arrangement was a novelty as late as the 1760s. Before then, a traveller who wanted a hot meal usually went to an inn or tavern offering a table d'hôte, the host's table. Diners sat together at a fixed hour and ate whatever the host had cooked, for a fixed charge. Latecomers found the best portions gone, and shy or unknown guests could be outmanoeuvred by regulars who reached for the dishes first.

The first establishments to call themselves restaurants did not set out to replace this system. The word originally named a restorative broth, a concentrated meat stock believed to strengthen people with weak constitutions. Shops selling these broths presented themselves as places of health rather than of pleasure. Customers, many of them delicate city dwellers, could arrive when they felt the need, sit at a small separate table and order a single bowl. Because the broth was treated as a remedy, these sellers could operate alongside the powerful guilds whose members held the right to sell many kinds of cooked food.

Over the following decades the menus lengthened. Broths were joined by eggs, fruit, rice puddings and eventually roast fowl, and the printed list of dishes with individual prices, the carte, became the defining feature. What attracted customers was not only the food but also control: they could decide when to eat, how much to spend and with whom to share a table.

A popular story holds that the restaurant was born from the French Revolution, when cooks who had served aristocratic households lost their employers and opened dining rooms for the public. The abolition of the guilds in 1791 certainly made it easier to open such businesses, and the number of restaurants in Paris grew sharply. But the basic form, with separate tables, flexible hours and a priced menu, already existed before 1789. The Revolution accelerated a change; it did not invent it.

Today a restaurant seems an obvious idea: you choose a time, sit at your own table, pick dishes from a printed list and pay a stated price for what you ate. Yet in Paris this arrangement was a novelty as late as the 1760s. Before then, a traveller who wanted a hot meal usually went to an inn or tavern offering a table d'hôte, the host's table. Diners sat together at a fixed hour and ate whatever the host had cooked, for a fixed charge. Latecomers found the best portions gone, and shy or unknown guests could be outmanoeuvred by regulars who reached for the dishes first.

The first establishments to call themselves restaurants did not set out to replace this system. The word originally named a restorative broth, a concentrated meat stock believed to strengthen people with weak constitutions. Shops selling these broths presented themselves as places of health rather than of pleasure. Customers, many of them delicate city dwellers, could arrive when they felt the need, sit at a small separate table and order a single bowl. Because the broth was treated as a remedy, these sellers could operate alongside the powerful guilds whose members held the right to sell many kinds of cooked food.

Over the following decades the menus lengthened. The abolition of the guilds in 1791 certainly made it easier to open such businesses, and the number of restaurants in Paris grew sharply. items.stimulus:
Employees are often told that loyalty is a virtue, and in ordinary circumstances it is. An organisation cannot function if its members leak every internal disagreement or treat each unpopular decision as a scandal. Colleagues who share plans, drafts and mistakes need to trust that these will not be broadcast. So anyone who reports their own employer to a regulator or a journalist owes the rest of us an explanation.

That explanation, however, is sometimes easy to give. Loyalty is not owed to a building or a logo but to the shared purpose that the organisation exists to serve: a hospital to heal, a bank to look after savings, a manufacturer to make safe and useful goods. When managers conceal practices that betray this purpose, such as falsified safety tests or hidden losses, the employee who exposes them is not abandoning the organisation. She is siding with what the organisation is supposed to be against the people currently misusing it.

This does not license every disclosure. Several conditions should normally be met. The harm at stake must be serious and fall on people outside the organisation, not merely on the pride of a manager. The evidence must be reliable rather than rumour. Internal channels should have been tried first, unless they are controlled by the very people involved or the delay would itself cause harm. And there must be a reasonable prospect that going public will help to stop the harm, rather than simply damaging reputations.

Where these conditions hold, the usual charge of disloyalty loses its force. It is the concealment, not the disclosure, that breaks faith with colleagues, customers and the public. Where they do not hold, the whistleblower may still be sincere, but sincerity alone does not justify the costs that disclosure imposes on innocent co-workers.

In Britain at the start of the twentieth century, campaigners for women's votes agreed on the goal but divided sharply over method. The largest organisation, the National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies, founded in 1897, relied on what its members called constitutional means: petitions, public meetings, letters to newspapers and patient lobbying of sympathetic members of Parliament. Its leaders believed that demonstrating women's reasonableness would steadily erode the argument that women were unfit for political life.

In 1903 a smaller group, the Women's Social and Political Union, adopted the slogan 'Deeds not words'. Its members at first interrupted political meetings and staged processions; later, frustrated by repeated parliamentary delays, some broke windows, cut telegraph wires and set fire to empty buildings. Imprisoned members went on hunger strike, and the authorities responded with force-feeding and, from 1913, a law that released weakened prisoners and re-arrested them once they had recovered.

The two approaches interacted in complicated ways. Militant actions brought the question enormous publicity, and newspapers that had ignored polite meetings filled their front pages. Yet opponents used the same headlines to claim that women had proved themselves too emotional to be trusted with the vote, and some sympathetic politicians said they could not be seen to give in to violence. Meanwhile, membership of the constitutional societies grew rapidly in the years of greatest militancy, partly because women who wanted the vote but disliked lawbreaking looked for an alternative.

When war broke out in 1914, the militant union suspended its campaign, and many suffragists turned to war work. In 1918 Parliament gave the vote to women over thirty who met a property qualification; equal voting terms with men followed in 1928. Historians still disagree about how much credit each strategy deserves, and some argue that the question itself is misleading, since the moderate campaign's apparent respectability may have depended partly on the contrast with the militants.

items.stimulus:
Ask a room of adults whether they wish they had learned a musical instrument as children, and most hands go up. Ask whether they intend to start now, and the hands come down. The usual excuse is that the window has closed: real musicians, we are told, begin before they can read, and anyone starting at forty is wasting their time.

This excuse confuses two different goals. If the aim is to become a concert soloist, then early training may well matter. But almost nobody who picks up a cello in middle age wants to play in a famous concert hall. They want to play a tune for their grandchildren, join a community orchestra, or simply spend an evening absorbed in something that is not a screen. For these goals, a late start is no obstacle at all.

Adults also have advantages that children lack. They choose to practise rather than being sent to their rooms to do it. They can understand why a technical exercise matters, and they can pay for good teaching. Most importantly, they are not being compared with prodigies at the school concert. Their progress is measured against who they were last month.

Then there is the effect on the mind. Learning an instrument demands attention, memory, coordination and patience all at once, a combination few other hobbies require. A friend of mine took up the piano at fifty-five, and within a year she said her memory was sharper than it had been for a decade. Clearly, then, learning an instrument protects adults against mental decline.

None of this means the process is easy. The first months are humbling, and fingers that type quickly can feel clumsy on strings. But being a beginner again is part of the value. Adults spend most of their lives doing things they are already good at. An instrument offers the rarer experience of becoming slowly, audibly better at something difficult, and that is worth more than any number of regrets about the lessons we never had.

items.stimulus:
Speaker 1: Our government spends billions on rockets while waiting lists for surgery grow longer every year. Cancel the next Mars mission and those lists could be cut. Space can wait; patients cannot. Public money should go first to needs that are urgent and certain, and only then to projects whose benefits are distant and uncertain.

Speaker 2: Space programmes are not a separate world from domestic needs. Weather satellites improve harvest planning and storm warnings, and satellite navigation underpins modern transport. Much of this technology began as government space research that no private firm would have funded at the time. Cutting space budgets today may mean losing the practical tools of tomorrow.

Speaker 3: When our country launched its first lunar probe, applications to university science courses rose for several years. Young people need ambitious public projects to imagine themselves into. I would not fund space instead of schools, but a modest space budget can do something for schools that a larger school budget alone cannot: it gives students a reason to study hard subjects.

Speaker 4: If space research is so valuable, private companies will pay for it, as some already do. The state should not use taxes to fund ventures that investors would back anyway, and where no firm sees a profit, that usually signals that the benefits are too small to justify the cost. Leave space to the market and keep public budgets for services the market will not provide.

items.stimulus:
A society that values tolerance faces an awkward question: should it tolerate people who reject tolerance itself? The problem, often associated with the philosopher Karl Popper, is sometimes called the paradox of tolerance. If a tolerant society extends unlimited tolerance to movements that aim to silence or persecute others, those movements may grow strong enough to destroy the tolerance that protected them. Unlimited tolerance, on this view, can undermine itself.

The tempting conclusion is that intolerant views should simply be banned. But this response creates difficulties of its own. Who decides which views count as intolerant? A label that begins by targeting genuine threats can be stretched to cover unpopular opinions, rival parties or awkward critics. A society that silences too readily may become the very thing it feared.

A more careful version of the argument distinguishes between expressing an intolerant idea and acting to impose it. As long as intolerant groups are willing to argue in public, to be answered, and to accept the results of fair procedures, the tolerant society can meet them with argument rather than force. Their ideas may be offensive, but they remain within the shared rules. The right to restrict them arises only when they abandon those rules: when they refuse debate, use intimidation or violence, or try to prevent others from speaking.

On this account, tolerance is not a principle of unlimited permission but something like a reciprocal agreement. Each party accepts the other's right to exist and to speak in exchange for the same acceptance. Those who break the agreement cannot then claim its protection, not because their opinions are wrong, but because they have stepped outside the arrangement that made the protection possible. The line is drawn at conduct, not at belief.

items.stimulus:
Civic buildings rarely just house officials; they also speak to the people who pass them. Rulers and governments have long used architecture to send messages about who holds authority and how that authority should be regarded.

Scale is the oldest of these messages. A town hall that rises above the surrounding houses, or a ministry approached by a long flight of steps, makes visitors feel physically smaller and slows them as they arrive. Many nineteenth-century city halls in Europe borrowed columns and triangular pediments from ancient temples, linking the new authorities to a past that was widely admired and implying that their power was as settled as stone.

Materials and placement carry meaning too. Expensive imported stone advertised wealth, and a building set at the end of a broad avenue could be seen from far away, so that the seat of power seemed to command the city. Some planners deliberately aligned streets so that every approach ended at the same official front.

Yet the message has not always been one of dominance. In the late twentieth century, several parliaments and city councils commissioned buildings with glass walls, open public galleries and entrances at street level. Their designers argued that transparency in architecture would express, and perhaps encourage, openness in government. Critics replied that a glass wall shows only what its owners choose to show, and that a visible debating chamber does not reveal decisions made in private offices.

Whether imposing or transparent, such buildings share one assumption: that the public reads architecture, even if it never puts the reading into words.

items.stimulus:
Speaker 1 (Mirela Santos, novelist): 'Leisure is not the reward for work; it is the part of life for which work exists. A society that forgets this ends up admiring exhaustion.'

Speaker 2 (Gideon Park, factory owner): 'Idle hours breed restlessness. Give people meaningful work and they will not need to be entertained; they will find their satisfaction in what they make.'

Speaker 3 (Lena Achterberg, union organiser): 'The weekend was not a gift from employers. It was won by people who insisted that time away from the workplace belonged to workers, not to the company.'

Speaker 4 (Ravi Okonjo, psychologist): 'Rest is not the opposite of productive work but one of its conditions. Minds that never pause make more errors, not more progress.'
items.question: Speaker 4 values rest mainly because it

improves the quality of people's work.
is the purpose for which people work.

items.stimulus: Six friends, Ana, Ben, Cara, Dev, Eli and Fay, arrive at a restaurant and sit down at random in the six equally spaced seats around a round table. Every possible seating arrangement is equally likely. Two people sit 'next to each other' if their seats are adjacent, and a person sits 'directly opposite' the person three seats away.
items.question: What is the probability that Ana and Ben sit next to each other?
items.explanation_ko: 1) 애나의 자리를 기준으로 고정하면 벤은 남은 5자리 중 하나에 똑같은 확률로 앉는다. 2) 그중 애나 옆자리는 2개이므로 확률 = 2/5. 오답: A 2/6으로 애나의 자리까지 셈에 넣은 값이다. B 옆자리를 하나만 센 값이다. C 1/6은 애나의 자리를 고정하지 않고 벤이 6자리 중 특정한 한 자리에 앉을 확률로 본 값이다. E 옆과 옆이 아닌 경우를 같은 확률로 본 값이다. 유형 팁: 원탁 확률은 한 사람의 자리를 고정하고 나머지의 선택지를 세면 간단해진다. → 정답 D

items.stimulus: Six friends, Ana, Ben, Cara, Dev, Eli and Fay, arrive at a restaurant and sit down at random in the six equally spaced seats around a round table. Every possible seating arrangement is equally likely. Two people sit 'next to each other' if their seats are adjacent, and a person sits 'directly opposite' the person three seats away.

items.explanation_ko: 1) 애나의 자리를 고정하면 벤이 앉을 수 있는 자리는 5개이고 맞은편 자리는 1개다. 2) 확률 = 1/5. 오답: A 분모에 애나의 자리를 포함했다. C 이웃할 확률이다. D 2/6으로 계산한 값이다. 유형 팁: 고정한 사람의 자리는 분모에서 뺀다. → 정답 B

items.stimulus: Six friends, Ana, Ben, Cara, Dev, Eli and Fay, arrive at a restaurant and sit down at random in the six equally spaced seats around a round table. Every possible seating arrangement is equally likely. Two people sit 'next to each other' if their seats are adjacent, and a person sits 'directly opposite' the person three seats away.
items.question: What is the probability that Ana sits between Ben and Cara, with Ben on one side of her and Cara on the other?
items.explanation_ko: 1) 애나의 양옆 두 자리에 앉을 두 사람은 나머지 5명 중 2명이다. 순서를 무시하면 경우의 수는 C(5,2) = 10이고 모두 같은 확률이다. 2) 그중 {벤, 캐라}는 1가지이므로 1/10. 순서를 따지면 (5 × 4 = 20가지 중 벤-캐라, 캐라-벤 2가지) 2/20 = 1/10로 같다. 오답: B 두 배로 잘못 센 값이다. C 벤-캐라의 순서 하나만 센 값이다. D 두 사건(벤이 옆, 캐라가 옆)을 독립으로 보고 2/5 × 2/5를 곱한 값이다. 유형 팁: 같은 자리를 다투는 사건은 독립이 아니므로 확률을 단순히 곱하면 안 된다. → 정답 A
